title: AI Orchestration is a team effort.
summary: AI Orchestration is a team effort. New Upwork research explores how leading organizations use a blended workforce to turn AI adoption into impact.
body_markdown:
by Jennifer Brett


### Key Insights


- **The emerging AI orchestrator is best understood as a team or cross-functional capability** . The work spans workflows, integration, validation, governance, business decisions, and measurement, making it difficult to contain in one job description.
- **AI operating maturity increases the need for flexible talent.** The share saying AI has increased their need for freelance or contingent talent rises from 72% of foundational organizations to 90% of advanced organizations, and advanced organizations are more likely to put that talent to work in orchestration.
- **The preferred AI workforce model is blended** . 70% of leaders expect to combine employees with freelance or contingent professionals for major AI initiatives


## How leading organizations use a blended workforce to turn AI adoption into impact.


The popular image of an AI orchestrator is a new kind of employee: one person who directs AI agents, improves prompts, and keeps automated work on track. In[Upwork’s Future Workforce Index 2026](https://www.upwork.com/research/research-future-workforce-index-2026) , we described the emerging AI orchestrator role: a worker who connects AI tools and agents to real workflows, applies judgment and oversight, and turns AI-enabled execution into business results. New research from the Upwork Research Institute evolves this idea: **The AI orchestrator is increasingly a team effort, not a single role** .


Orchestration connects AI tools and outputs to workflows, human judgment, operating standards, and measurable results. That work crosses technical, operational, governance, and talent boundaries. It may have a clear leader, but it rarely fits within one role or one source of talent. The organizations furthest ahead are formalizing orchestration across teams and extending their capacity with outside specialists.


This changes the hiring story around AI. **More AI-mature organizations do not appear to grow out of needing flexible talent as their internal capabilities improve** . 90% of advanced organizations, as classified in Upwork’s AI operating maturity model, say AI has increased their need for freelance or contingent talent, compared with 72% of foundational organizations. External expertise is becoming part of the AI operating model.


## AI adoption is no longer the main divide


**Basic AI use is already widespread** . 65% of surveyed organizations have embedded AI across multiple functions or scaled it organization-wide. Another 29% use it regularly in at least some teams or functions. Even among organizations classified as foundational in Upwork’s AI operating maturity model, 88% use AI regularly somewhere in the business.


Impact is less evenly distributed. 91% report a measurable benefit somewhere in the organization, but only 35% report significant, measurable impact across the business. The gap is no longer mainly about access to AI. It is about whether an organization can turn scattered AI usage into a structured, repeatable system for changing how work gets done.


**That system is orchestration** . Adding an AI tool to an existing process may make one task faster, but it does not resolve weak handoffs, unclear accountability, inconsistent review, or the distance between an AI output and a business decision. People must redesign the workflow around the technology and improve it after launch.


## AI orchestration is a cross-functional capability


**Business leaders define orchestration through a wide range of responsibilities (see figure 1)** . 57% include identifying workflows suited to AI. Half include improving prompts and processes over time. 48% include validating AI-generated outputs, 47% monitoring risk and compliance, 46% redesigning workflows, 45% connecting outputs to business decisions, and 45% measuring impact.


**Figure 1: The range of responsibilities underlying AI orchestration**


No single specialist is likely to bring deep technical knowledge, process expertise, risk oversight, and business context to every initiative. A company may appoint an orchestration leader, but the capability is still likely to be distributed.


**Organizations are already using several structures to cover this type of work** . 35% have a dedicated orchestration role or team, 28% formally assign the responsibility to existing employees, 26% rely on employees handling it informally, and 11% primarily use external specialists. The important distinction is not the org chart. It is whether the responsibilities are explicit, coordinated, and measured.


The need is widely recognized: **87% say orchestration capabilities will be essential or very important to getting value from AI over the next year** . Yet more than a quarter still handle the work informally. When ownership is unclear, integration, review, risk management, and measurement can fall between teams. Formal orchestration turns those activities into a managed process instead of a collection of individual efforts.


## AI maturity shows the value of an operating system


Upwork’s AI operating maturity model measures five capabilities: broad AI deployment, clear business outcomes, KPIs for AI initiatives, meaningful workflow redesign, and structured ownership of orchestration. Organizations meeting zero or one criterion are foundational, those meeting two or three are developing, and those meeting four or five are advanced. These groups account for 28%, 37%, and 35% of respondents, respectively.


‍ **The differences in AI outcomes across these groups are notable (see figure 2)** . 7% of foundational organizations report significant business-wide AI impact, compared with 33% of developing organizations and 61% of advanced organizations. Advanced organizations are also more likely to be hiring for workflow redesign or AI implementation. The pattern shows an association between AI operating discipline and reported impact.


**Figure 2: Selected outcomes by AI operating maturity**


The obstacles to getting value from AI also change with maturity. Foundational organizations more often cite insufficient employee skills and problems with data quality, access, or integration. Advanced organizations report fewer of these basic capability barriers, while governance becomes more prominent. 47% cite regulatory, privacy, security, or compliance concerns, compared with 35% of foundational organizations. As AI reaches more workflows, orchestration has to manage a larger system and a broader set of consequences.


## Flexible talent expands orchestration capacity & capabilities


A common assumption is that organizations depend less on external AI talent as they build internal expertise. The survey points in the opposite direction. **The share saying AI has increased their need for freelance or contingent talent rises at every maturity level** : 72% of foundational organizations, 84% of developing organizations, and 90% of advanced organizations.


**Figure 3: Need for flexible talent increases with AI operating maturity**


**Advanced organizations are also more likely to put that talent to work in orchestration** . 66% currently use freelance or contract professionals for orchestration, compared with 49% of foundational organizations. 49% invest in freelance AI implementation talent, compared with 29% of foundational organizations. Across the full sample, 83% say AI has already increased their need for flexible talent, 81% expect that need to increase during the next six months, and 90% are likely to use freelance or contingent professionals for AI implementation. **Orchestration creates demand for changing combinations of expertise** . A workflow may need an automation engineer during integration and a compliance specialist to build a governance model. The need changes as an initiative moves from design to deployment and oversight. Flexible talent lets companies add capabilities when the work requires them.


‍ **The preferred workforce model is blended** . 70% of leaders say they are most likely to combine employees with freelance or contingent talent for major AI initiatives, and that preference is consistent across maturity levels. Employees supply company knowledge, continuity, and accountability. External specialists provide scarce skills, implementation capacity, and experience from solving similar problems in other settings.


The findings do not show that freelance talent causes greater maturity. They show that strong internal capability and external expertise are complements. As companies move from isolated use cases to interconnected workflows, their need for orchestration can expand faster than one team can absorb.


## Four practices to build orchestration


What can organizations learn from the most advanced AI operators? Below are 4 best practices from leading AI implementers to turn AI adoption into business impact.


1. **Define the result before selecting the tool.** Give each initiative a business outcome and a way to measure it.
2. **Map and assess the whole workflow.** Identify inputs, decisions, handoffs, review points, risks, and accountability before adding AI.
3. **Assign clear orchestration ownership.** Name who coordinates implementation, validation, governance, and improvement, even when the work is distributed.
4. **Build a blended capability.** Keep business context and accountability inside the organization while using external specialists for scarce expertise and variable implementation needs.


The next phase of AI will be shaped less by who has access to the technology than by who can coordinate the work around it. That is the real role of the AI orchestrator. A leader may own it, but a blended and cross-functional team delivers it.


‍


## Methodology


The data is based on a survey of 750 U.S.-based business leaders (director plus seniority) from August to September 2026. The survey was fielded externally by McGuire Research.


The Upwork AI Operating Maturity Model measures organizations’ progress from isolated AI adoption to scaled, outcome-oriented operating transformation. We define AI operating maturity based on capability thresholds that we have established across five organizational dimensions: breadth of deployment, clarity of business outcomes, measurement, workflow redesign, and structured orchestration. Organizations meeting zero or one of these thresholds are classified as foundational, those meeting two or three as developing, and those meeting four or five as advanced. Its five dimensions reflect capabilities identified in established AI maturity, governance, and value-realization frameworks (such as[Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agents/adoption-maturity-model/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ,[McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-how-organizations-are-rewiring-to-capture-value?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , and[NIST](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ). The model is designed as a concise, survey-based operating index rather than a comprehensive assessment of every element of AI readiness.


Basic AI adoption is already high across all three segments. Even among foundational organizations, 88% report using AI regularly somewhere in the business. This indicates that the AI operating maturity model is reflective of how AI is utilized within an organization after basic adoption.


AI operating maturity does not rise consistently with company size. Very large organizations are most likely to be advanced, but very small organizations also perform strongly. This suggests that resources and scale can help, but they are not prerequisites for maturity. Organizational focus, agility, workflow redesign, and clear ownership may matter as much as employee count.

### About The Upwork Research Institute


The world of work is not the same as it was just a few years ago, and leaders are facing new challenges as a result. The old work playbook is gone, and in its place are new debates and decisions around workforce location, worker arrangements, flexibility, and the role of AI in how work gets done. Leaders do not need to navigate this new world of work on their own.


The Upwork Research Institute is committed to studying the fundamental shifts in the workforce and providing business leaders with the tools and insights they need to navigate the here and now while preparing their organizations for the future. Using proprietary platform data, global survey research, partnerships, and academic collaborations, the Institute produces evidence-based insights to help create the blueprint for the new way of work.


### About the author


[Jennifer Brett](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jennifermbrett/) is the managing director of The Upwork Research Institute, where she leads research and thought leadership on the future of work, including AI, flexible talent, and evolving workforce models. She is a research and insights leader with more than 15 years of experience translating data, market signals, and human behavior into strategies, narratives, and business impact. Jennifer has held senior insights leadership roles at Attentive and LinkedIn across the U.S. and Europe, and previously served as an industry analyst at Google. She holds a Ph.D. in political science from Trinity College Dublin, with academic training in research design and quantitative and qualitative methods.
